A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same theoretical work despite the changed title and reorganized sections. Their complete main texts, equations, payoff tables, and Appendices A-C support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical bounds, constructed game examples, and proofs. Neither its main text nor its appendices report original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: v3 retains the theoretical results and proof appendices and adds explanatory discussion. It reports no original empirical outcomes.

M1.justification: The generalized principal-agent model, learning interactions, approximate-best-response reductions, and Appendix A's Algorithm 1 are retained. Foregrounding the general model and clarifying feedback do not change the procedure.

E1.justification: Neither version uses training or evaluation datasets. Bayesian persuasion, Stackelberg games, and contract design remain the same theoretical applications.

E2.justification: Neither version reports an empirical comparison against baselines. Newly cited research is discussed as related work, not evaluated as additional comparison methods.

E3.justification: Neither version presents an experimental evaluation protocol. Time horizons, regret parameters, and game configurations remain part of the same theoretical analysis.

E4.justification: The mean-based exploitation example and the two-action tightness example, including their supporting proofs, are retained. No ablation, robustness experiment, or additional case analysis is introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Expectations and regret bounds are theoretical quantities rather than empirical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The payoff matrices, derived utility bounds, and conclusions of the matched examples and corollaries are unchanged. There are no added or revised empirical result entries.

T1.justification: The reduction theorems, approximate-response bounds, assumptions, application corollaries, and Appendices A-C proofs match after renumbering. The generalized regret notation and expanded model explanation do not introduce new mathematics.

C1.justification: The three headline results and their application scope remain unchanged. Novelty claims are qualified: v1 presents learning-agent contract design and persuasion as previously unstudied, whereas v3 describes refinements of contract-design results and acknowledges concurrent persuasion research.

C2.justification: New Section 6 explains why conditioning deviations on both signals and recommended actions lets no-swap-regret constrain a principal using time-varying strategies, while ordinary no-regret may not. The complete-information restriction and private-information caveat were already stated in v1.

D1.justification: Appendix A's pseudocode is unchanged. No implementation parameters, computational resources, reproducibility instructions, or code/data access information are added or revised.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises priority positioning by acknowledging Guruganesh et al. on contract design and Jain and Perchet on concurrent persuasion research, replacing v1's assertion that these settings had not been studied with learning agents. It also adds Arunachaleswaran et al. and Kumar et al. The Gan et al. title/year update refers to the same arXiv work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introductory framing are rewritten around generalized principal-agent problems. The model exposition is substantially reordered to introduce the general framework before persuasion, approximate response moves into the reduction section, and a concluding Discussion section is added.

P2.justification: v3 adds a boxed presentation of the existing general learning interaction, relocates the persuasion and cheap-talk boxes, and moves existing payoff tables with the surrounding material. The table contents and Appendix A algorithm display remain unchanged; there is no substantial visual redesign.

improvement.justification: v3 improves clarity through the general-model-first organization and Section 6's explanation of the regret distinction. Its acknowledgment of prior contract-design and concurrent persuasion work also makes contribution attribution more precise. These are useful improvements to exposition and positioning, while the mathematical results and appendix proofs remain unchanged.
